name: Greek Revival

revival_periods.note: The Columbian Exposition returns the colossal portico to American building, now at institutional and banking scale, in stone or terracotta over steel.
Greek Revival is quietly absorbed into the market category 'Colonial', producing the two-storey pedimented entry porch that is proportionally neither.

geography.hearth: Philadelphia, then upstate New York and the Western Reserve

lineage.note: THE canonical reference edge in this taxonomy. No American builder had any line of transmission from Athens: no craftsman, no apprenticeship, no continuous trade, not even a surviving Greek building any of them had seen. What crossed was measured drawings - Stuart and Revett's Antiquities of Athens (1762-1830) - reproduced at fourth hand in carpenters' handbooks. This is quotation of an ancestor the style never descended from, and modelling it as descent would be false.

The actual mechanism, and it is embarrassingly literal. Asher Benjamin published The Country Builder's Assistant (1797) and The American Builder's Companion (1806) as Federal manuals, then reissued the same enterprise as The Architect, or Practical House Carpenter (1830) with Grecian plates. Same author, same audience, same trade, same moulding planes - a new set of profiles. Minard Lafever's Modern Builder's Guide (1833) and Beauties of Modern Architecture (1835) completed the retooling. The transmission is the pattern book and the carpenter who owned it.

And it is a proportional revolt before it is an ornamental one. Federal had thinned American classicism until it was a membrane: 7/8-inch muntins, 4-inch cornices, columns at ten and eleven diameters, ornament glued on as composition castings. Greek Revival answers with mass - baseless Doric at six diameters, an entablature a quarter as deep as the column is tall, trim boards six to twelve inches wide. Adamesque delicacy came to look effete and, worse, English.

The professional channel, distinct from the carpenter channel. Benjamin Henry Latrobe trained in England inside the British Greek Revival and brought it to Philadelphia with the Bank of Pennsylvania (1798-1801); his pupils William Strickland and, through Strickland, Thomas U. Walter carried it into the American profession. Every high-style American Grecian building descends through this line rather than from the handbooks.

Explicit in the period literature: Greek is claimed as the purer, earlier, freer source and Roman as its imperial corruption. This is also a quiet argument against Jefferson, whose Roman republic is displaced by an older Greek one.

description.short: The first American national style: a Greek temple, known only from measured drawings and carpenters' handbooks, pressed into service as farmhouse, bank, courthouse and plantation seat across two-thirds of a continent between 1825 and 1860.
description.long:
Greek Revival is the node this taxonomy exists to model correctly, because it is the clearest case in the whole of American building where what a style claims and where it comes from are two entirely different things. What it claims is Athens. What it descends from is Asher Benjamin's pattern book, and the descent is documented down to the individual plate. Formally the style is a set of substitutions performed on the Federal house: the elliptical fanlight becomes a rectangular transom; the slender colonnette becomes a baseless Doric column six diameters tall; the four-inch cornice becomes an entablature a quarter as deep as the column is high; the wall's corner boards swell into pilasters; the attic storey is lit through small windows cut into the frieze itself; and the roof is often rotated so its gable faces the street as a pediment. The result is a building that has more in common with a Greek temple in its silhouette than in any other respect, since it is generally made of white-painted pine over a braced frame and heated by cast-iron stoves.

The distinction between reference and descent is the substance of the node, so state it plainly. No American builder in 1835 had a line of transmission from Greek practice. There was no craft continuity, no apprenticeship lineage, no surviving Greek building on the continent, and until well into the nineteenth century almost no American had seen one in person; Greece itself was under Ottoman rule and effectively closed. What crossed the Atlantic was paper: James Stuart and Nicholas Revett's Antiquities of Athens, published in volumes from 1762, measured on site and engraved - and then abridged, simplified and re-engraved in the handbooks that a rural carpenter could actually afford. The style therefore quotes an ancestor it never descended from. Its real ancestor is the one it was reacting against. Asher Benjamin, who taught two generations of New England housewrights how to build Federal, published The Architect, or Practical House Carpenter in 1830 with the Grecian orders in it, and the same men who had been running Adamesque beads went out and ran Doric mouldings the following season. Minard Lafever's Modern Builder's Guide (1833) and The Beauties of Modern Architecture (1835) did the same for New York and the whole territory its canal system opened. Parallel to the handbooks ran a professional line - Latrobe out of the English Greek Revival, then Strickland, then Walter - which produced the banks and the marble porticoes. Two channels, one style, and neither of them touches Greece.

The conditions that made it national were political, economic and technological at once, and they arrived together. Politically: the Greek War of Independence (1821-32) made Greece a live cause in American newspapers at the exact moment when a young republic wanted a founding image that was neither English nor royal, and the natural rhetorical move - we are the new Athens - could be built. Economically: the Erie Canal opened in 1825, the Western Reserve and the Old Northwest filled with New England and New York settlers, and the cotton boom capitalised the Lower South, so an enormous quantity of building happened in one generation with money and without inherited local traditions. Technologically: the water-powered sash and blind mill, cheap machine-cut nails, and after 1833 the balloon frame made it possible for a small crew to raise a broad flat-trimmed wooden building fast; wide trim in clear pine was cheap, and white lead paint over it read at a quarter mile as marble. This is the first American style to be genuinely continental, and it is also the first whose spread is explained better by transport infrastructure than by taste.

What is it like to stand before one. Weight is the first fact - the reverse of Federal in every dimension. The eave line no longer runs as a thin shadow but sits as a horizontal band a foot and a half deep, and everything under it feels held down. If there is a portico it goes the full height of the block, so the columns commit the whole building rather than decorating its door, and standing between them you are inside a room without walls, on a stone or wood platform raised three or four steps above the grade. The wall itself has almost no incident: broad flat pilasters at the corners, wide plain casings, and a door assembly that is a rectangle inside a rectangle, transom above and sidelights beside, all under a heavy flat entablature. In the frieze, if you look, there are small horizontal windows, and they are the tell that the attic is habitable - the most quietly ingenious detail in the whole American kit, since it lets a full storey exist without disturbing a pediment. Inside, the rooms are taller than Federal rooms and much plainer: heavy symmetrical architraves with corner blocks, deep plain baseboards, black marble mantels of two square posts and a slab. It is a serious, slightly humourless, extremely durable architecture, and the reason it looks like the default image of an American house is that for thirty-five years it very nearly was.

defining_characteristics: Full-height portico, pilastered antae, or a pedimented gable-front used as the governing facade gesture - column height equals the full height of the block it fronts
Greek orders only: baseless fluted Doric, Greek Ionic, or the Tower-of-the-Winds Corinthian; no Roman arches, no domes, no Composite
Deep entablature, one quarter to one fifth of column height, carried as a continuous horizontal band around the building
Low roof pitch (4:12 to 6:12) so that a gable reads as a pediment, with the cornice returning or running level across the gable base
Rectangular transom over the entrance with flanking sidelights within a pilastered surround; elliptical fanlights eliminated
Broad, flat, unmoulded trim: corner pilasters, wide window casings, plain frieze board - ornament by profile and mass, not by relief carving
Frieze-band attic windows where an upper half-storey is habitable
diagnostic_tells: Small horizontal windows set into the frieze board directly under the eave: no other American style does this, and it settles the identification instantly

Greek Revival versus Colonial Revival portico at fifty feet - Greek Revival columns run the full facade height and carry a deep entablature; the Colonial Revival entry porch is one storey against a two-storey wall and has a thin cornice
Doric columns without bases, sitting directly on the porch deck; a base under a Doric column means Roman, which means Jeffersonian or a later revival
Door transom rectangular, not elliptical - the single fastest Federal/Greek Revival discriminator on a plain house
The house turned gable-end to the road, so the pediment faces the traveller; a Federal or Georgian house of the same size faces the road broadside
Cornice returns clipped short on the gable ends of a vernacular example - the cheapest possible gesture toward a pediment, and everywhere in the Northeast

distinguished_from.difference: A proportional inversion before an ornamental one. Federal attenuates - columns at 10-11 diameters, cornices at 1/25 of facade height, muntins under 7/8 inch. Greek Revival thickens - columns at 6-7 diameters, entablature at 1/4 to 1/5 of column height, trim boards 6-12 inches wide. If the trim looks heavy and the transom is rectangular, it is Greek Revival even in the absence of a single column.

Both build porticoes, but the vocabularies are mutually exclusive. Jefferson's classicism is Roman: bases under the columns, arches, domes, semicircular windows. Greek Revival forbids all four. Jeffersonian buildings argue from measured Roman antiquity via Palladio; Greek Revival argues from Stuart and Revett and reaches ten thousand carpenters who never heard of either.

The 1893-1940 revival uses colossal orders on masses of a size no antebellum builder attempted, in stone or terracotta over steel frames, with plate glass and Roman as often as Greek detail. Scale and material give it away; so does the fact that its columns are usually round-tapered mill-made shafts rather than built-up staves.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Greek orders with the module equal to the lower column diameter, taken at second or third hand from Stuart and Revett through Benjamin and Lafever. Because the source is a handbook rather than a building, the proportions are executed accurately at the level of the order and freely at the level of the building - a temple front applied to a domestic plan that owes nothing to Greece.
typical_ratios: Greek Doric column 5.5-7 lower diameters tall (Parthenon Doric is 5.5; American handbook Doric commonly 6-7)
Greek Ionic 8.5-9.5 diameters; Tower-of-the-Winds Corinthian about 10
Entablature depth 1/4 to 1/5 of column height - the single most diagnostic ratio in the style
Entablature subdivision architrave : frieze : cornice approximately 3 : 3 : 2
Pediment height 1/4.5 to 1/5.5 of its span (roof pitch 4:12 to 6:12)
Trim board widths: corner pilasters 8-14 inches, window casing 4-6 inches, frieze board 10-20 inches
Column height equals full facade height of the block it fronts, without exception in canonical work
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even intercolumniation of 2.25-2.75 diameters across the portico, set by the order and then imposed on the wall behind; on gable-front vernacular houses the rhythm is a simple 2 or 3 bay front with a side-hall door in the end bay, and the asymmetry of that door is tolerated because the pediment supplies the symmetry.

massing_affinities.note: The definitive American solution: keep the temple block pure and put the bedrooms and kitchen in lower recessed flankers.
The style's largest demographic contribution - rotating the ordinary house ninety degrees so its gable becomes a pediment, at no extra cost.
The Upland South and Midwest workhorse under Grecian trim.
New York, Brooklyn and Philadelphia rows of the 1830s-40s: brownstone or brick fronts with heavy Grecian door enframements.

constraints.statement: Portico column height must equal the full height of the facade it fronts, measured from porch deck to the underside of the main entablature. A two-storey block with one-storey columns is not Greek Revival; it is Colonial Revival or a later hybrid. Columns must be 5.5-7 lower diameters for Doric, 8.5-9.5 for Ionic.

Entablature depth must be 1/4 to 1/5 of column height, subdivided architrave : frieze : cornice at approximately 3 : 3 : 2. A cornice thinner than 1/8 of column height reads as Federal or Colonial Revival regardless of the columns below it.

test.note: 1/4 to 1/5 of column height. The 3:3:2 architrave:frieze:cornice subdivision and the under-1/8-reads-as-Federal clause stay prose.

constraints.statement: Where an upper half-storey is habitable it must be lit by frieze-band windows set within the entablature, no taller than one third of the frieze depth and aligned with the bays below. Dormers on the principal roof slope are forbidden; a frieze window and a dormer must never appear on the same elevation.

test.note: Tests the 'dormers forbidden on the principal roof slope' clause. Frieze-band window height relative to frieze depth (max one third), bay alignment, and the frieze-window/dormer mutual exclusion on one elevation are left as prose -- no vocabulary variable expresses frieze depth or per-elevation window/dormer co-occurrence.

constraints.statement: Greek vocabulary is exclusive: no round-headed arches, no domes, no elliptical fanlights, no columns with bases under a Doric order, no Composite capitals. The entrance must be a rectangular opening with a rectangular transom, sidelights optional, inside a pilastered surround.

Main roof pitch 4:12 to 6:12 so that any gable reads as a pediment (height 1/4.5 to 1/5.5 of span). Where no full pediment is built, the cornice must return at least 12 inches onto the gable end. Pitches above 8:12 push the building toward Gothic Revival.

test.note: Tests the 4:12-6:12 roof-pitch range. The pediment-height ratio and the 12in cornice-return-length rule (for a house with no full pediment) have no matching vocabulary variables and stay prose.

exemplars.name: Andalusia
exemplars.note: Thomas Ustick Walter's Doric temple front added to a 1794 house built for John Craig, acquired by Nicholas Biddle c. 1814 and turned to face the Delaware. The manifesto building of the American Greek Revival, by the man who later built the U.S. Capitol dome.

exemplars.name: Rose Hill Mansion
exemplars.location: Geneva (town of Fayette), Seneca County, New York
exemplars.note: Hexastyle Ionic portico with fully pedimented gable and Ionic colonnades on the flanking single-storey wings; builders working directly from Lafever's plates. National Historic Landmark.

exemplars.name: Berry Hill
exemplars.note: Begun 1842; architect John Evans Johnson, builder Josiah Dabbs. Octastyle Doric portico with an entablature six and a half feet deep, correctly detailed with triglyphs, metopes and guttae, plus matching tetrastyle Doric dependencies.

exemplars.name: Oak Alley
exemplars.note: Begun 1837. A peripteral colonnade of 28 stuccoed brick Doric columns on all four sides - the Greek temple hybridised with the Creole gallery house, and structurally a shading device before it is a quotation.

sources: Talbot Hamlin, Greek Revival Architecture in America (1944)
Roger G. Kennedy, Greek Revival America (1989)
Asher Benjamin, The Architect, or Practical House Carpenter (1830)
Minard Lafever, The Beauties of Modern Architecture (1835)
James Stuart and Nicholas Revett, The Antiquities of Athens (1762-1830)

proportion_packs.note: The single most consequential choice in this batch. Benjamin's Doric of The Practical House Carpenter (Boston, 1830), Example No. 3, is encoded as a STANDALONE order with overlay_of deliberately null, not as a delta on Vignola -- Benjamin says so himself in his preface, quoted in the pack: the Doric is the one order where 'the Greek and Roman creeds' are irreconcilable, so treating it as a Vignola overlay 'would be fiction' (docs/open-questions.md item 11). This pack's column stands 14 semidiameter-modules, i.e. 7 diameters -- the upper end of the style's own stated 'Greek Doric column 5.5-7 lower diameters' -- and it is architecturally the right choice specifically because this is Greek Revival, not Federal: Benjamin's OTHER 1816 Roman Doric (9 diameters, in the American Builder's Companion) is a legitimate delta on Vignola but is explicitly not what built this style, per the pack's own authority note.

A DELIBERATE SUBSTITUTION, STATED PLAINLY. This corpus gives Benjamin's Doric standalone Greek-order treatment but not his Ionic or Corinthian -- his 1816 Ionic and Corinthian overlays are the Federal-era Roman orders and their own authority notes say outright that 'where a house is Greek Revival rather than Federal, this pack is the wrong one.' No Benjamin or dedicated Greek Ionic pack exists in this corpus, so plain Vignola is bound here as an honest general-reasoning stand-in rather than a fabricated Grecian citation: Vignola's Ionic column runs 9 diameters, which happens to fall inside the style's own stated Greek Ionic range of 8.5-9.5, so the proportions hold even though the source is Roman rather than Greek. Bound at all because the style names Greek Ionic as a legitimate alternate order alongside baseless Doric (defining_characteristics) and because greek-revival-southern-plantation's exemplars use it directly.

Bind the wall_section_greek_revival / casing_greek_revival family -- the cleanest, most direct fit in this whole batch. The pack's own comparison names the diagnostic: Greek Revival's baseboard runs 10 1/4 in in only two members (against Georgian's 6 7/8 in in three and Federal's 6 1/8 in in three) because 'the pedestal has been abandoned entirely,' which is exactly the heavier, plainer, corner-blocked interior the style file itself describes -- 'heavy symmetrical architraves with corner blocks, deep plain baseboards, black marble mantels of two square posts and a slab.'

Governs the entrance void beneath constraint c04's hard exclusion: rectangular transom only, no elliptical fanlight, sidelights optional, all inside a pilastered surround -- the single fastest Federal/Greek Revival discriminator the style names for itself. Ranked ahead of sash-light here, the reverse of the Federal ordering, because the diagnostic weight in this style sits on transom shape and frieze-window placement, not on muntin width.

Still governs the window module and muntin coordination, but it is demoted relative to opening-proportion because Greek Revival, unlike Federal, does not stake its identity on sash pattern -- the style file's own diagnostic_tells list frieze windows, transom shape and portico proportion, and never mentions muntin count.

Governs the full-height portico composition and the bay rhythm the portico sets for the wall behind it (intercolumniation 2.25-2.75 diameters, per the style's own proportional_system). On the gable-front vernacular form the pack's odd-bay-count logic gives way to the style's own tolerated asymmetric side-hall door, which the pediment is stated to resolve compositionally rather than by bay symmetry.

Bound, but its usual Georgian/Federal job -- diminishing upper-storey window height so the eye reads a hierarchy -- is largely absent here: Greek Revival unifies the whole facade height behind one continuous entablature rather than stepping it down, and the style's own typical_ratios give no diminution ratio at all (unlike federal-style's explicit 0.80-0.90 / 0.60-0.75). Bound chiefly for the ceiling-height figure, which this pack's own authority note names directly ('Greek Revival 10-12 ft'), and for the frieze-band attic storey, where a habitable half-storey is lit through the entablature rather than through a dormer (constraint c03).

Bound for rooms that are 'taller than Federal rooms and much plainer' but still formally proportioned by a pattern-book carpenter rather than accumulated by habit -- the style's own description language. Benjamin-corinthian and benjamin-tuscan were both considered for a third bound order (the style names a Tower-of-the-Winds Corinthian as a legitimate third Greek order) and deliberately not bound at this parent level, to keep the same primary/secondary discipline georgian-colonial-american uses; the Corinthian is promoted instead on greek-revival-southern-plantation, where the style text and the corpus's own applies_to cross-reference both name it explicitly.

WP-4.6: bound secondary, and deliberately not primary. American Greek Revival work was built from Benjamin and Lafever, not from the Parthenon, and `benjamin-doric` is the pack that describes what the carpenters actually did. This pack is bound beside it as the archaeological order those buildings were imitating, so a plan can be checked against both -- what was built, and what it was reaching for. Where they disagree the disagreement is the finding.
